El teorema de aproximación universal: un: The universal approximation theorem: a sufficiently wide hidden layer approximates any continuous function, adding steps like a Riemann sum.
El teorema dice que <strong>existe</stro: The theorem says that a network approximating the function exists, not that it can be found by training, nor how many neurons will be needed. And often a very great many are needed: an extremely wide hidden layer may require a number of neurons that grows exponentially with the dimension. In practice it comes out far cheaper to stack several narrow layers than to put in a single immense one, and that —that depth is more efficient than width— is what gave deep learning its name.

La estructura de este tema es, sin exage: The structure of this topic is, without exaggeration, that of any current model. A language model is a stack of blocks in which what weighs most are dense layers exactly like these, with a non-linearity between them. The size, the particular activation and what is put around them change, but the operation the machine executes most of the time is still multiplying a matrix by a vector and applying a function component by component.

Que dos capas resolvían el XOR se sabía: That two layers solved XOR had always been known; what there was not was a way of training them, and that is the real reason for the halt that followed Minsky and Papert's book of 1969. The universal approximation theorem was proved by George Cybenko in 1989 for sigmoids, and Kurt Hornik generalised it in 1991 to any non-polynomial activation, which made it clear that the sigmoid had nothing special about it: the essential thing was not being a polynomial. And at that very moment the way of training these networks had existed since 1986, and it is the next topic.

It reads: “vector a is sigma of, W times vector x, plus vector b”.

If the input has $n$ numbers and the layer has $m$ neurons, then $W$ is an $m \times n$ matrix —one row per neuron, one column per input—, $\vec b$ has $m$ components and so does the output $\vec a$. The sigmoid is applied component by component, not to the sum of them all.

That is all. A network is a handful of these, chained: the output of one is the input of the next.
